AGA Clinical Practice Update on Surveillance of Pancreatic Cystic Lesions and Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Older Adults
  • Source: Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2026
  • Topic: Surveillance cessation criteria for pancreatic cysts and liver cancer in elderly patients
  • Author(s): Das KK, Serper M, Vege SS
Pancreatic Cystic Lesions (PCL) Surveillance Overview
  • Up to 26%–38% of patients >70 years have incidental PCLs on imaging
  • Vast majority are indolent
  • Some may develop into malignancy
  • Multiple guidelines exist for screening/surveillance
  • Few recommendations on when to stop surveillance
Key Surveillance Thresholds (IAP Criteria)
  • Growth rate of concern: ≥3 mm/year or ≥6 mm in 2 years
  • Worrisome features and high-risk stigmata define progression risk
Best Practice Advice 1: High Comorbidity = Stop Surveillance
  • AACCI ≥3–5 → counsel against routine PCL surveillance
  • Low attributable mortality to pancreatic cancer in this population
  • High intervention risks outweigh benefits
Supporting Evidence
  • Up to 75% of resected PCLs harbor only low-grade dysplasia (LGD) on final pathology
  • Pancreatic resection carries:
  • 1%–4% mortality even in expert centers
  • 40%–50% adverse event rate
  • 17.1% new-onset diabetes after Whipple
  • 23.7% new-onset diabetes after distal pancreatectomy
AACCI Impact Studies
  • AACCI ≥7: median survival only 43 months
  • AACCI ≥7: 11-fold risk of non-IPMN-related death within 3 years
  • High-risk patients (AACCI ≥3) with low-risk cyst:
  • Non-PC mortality: subdistribution HR 3.96 [95% CI, 2.98–5.26]
  • PC mortality: subdistribution HR 2.35 [95% CI, 0.14–38.82] (not significant)
Best Practice Advice 2: Age >65, Small Stable Cysts → Consider Stopping
  • Age >65 years
  • Cyst size ≤15 mm
  • Stable for 5 years (no growth ≥3 mm/year or 6 mm/2 years)
  • No worrisome features or high-risk stigmata (IAP-defined)
Evidence for Cessation
  • Large international cohort (3844 patients, median surveillance 53 months):
  • Patients ≥65 with lesions ≤15 mm after 5 years: standardized incidence ratio 0.95 [95% CI, 0.11–3.42]
  • All-cause mortality: 4.9% (n=79)
  • IPMN disease-specific mortality: 0.3% (n=5)
  • Patients >16 times more likely to die of other causes
  • Korean cohort: patients with PCLs ≤1.0 cm (n=501) → only 4.8% developed worrisome features with prolonged surveillance
  • Multicenter cohort (577 patients): 108 with stable PCLs ≤1.5 cm for >5 years → only 1 (0.9%) developed pancreatic cancer
Best Practice Advice 3: Age >75, Larger Stable Cysts → Discuss Cessation
  • Age >75 years
  • Cyst size <30 mm
  • Stable for 5 years (no growth ≥3 mm/year or 6 mm/2 years)
  • No worrisome features or high-risk stigmata
Evidence
  • International cohort: patients ≥75 with cysts <3 cm → standardized incidence ratio 1.12 [95% CI, 0.23–3.39]
  • Surveillance may be discontinued if patient understands small, population-specific risk of future PC or HGD
Best Practice Advice 4: New Comorbidities During Surveillance → Stop
  • Development of significant comorbidities (AACCI ≥3–5)
  • May preclude surgical resection at any time
  • Applies even with prior worrisome features or high-risk stigmata
  • No evidence of HGD or PC required for discontinuation discussion
Purpose of Surveillance
  • Goal is curative surgical resection if advanced neoplasia identified
  • No benefit/harm possible if patient cannot tolerate intervention
Tools for Life Expectancy Assessment
  • Combined Lee Schonberg 4–14 Year Mortality Index
  • Suemoto 10-year International Mortality Index
  • eFrailty.org (https://efrailty.hsl.harvard.edu/index.html)
Best Practice Advice 5: Post-Resection Surveillance (No HGD/PC)
  • Remnant pancreas surveillance can continue per BPA 2 and 3
  • Includes surveillance period preceding resection
  • Discussion of cessation after 5 years stability
  • Applies to patients with no evidence of HGD or PC on final pathology
Rationale
  • Frequent surgery for ultimately low-grade/benign disease
  • High upfront surgical morbidity
  • Long-term risks of endocrine/exocrine insufficiency
Caveats
  • Some guidelines recommend indefinite follow-up if surgically fit
  • Heterogeneity stems from lack of definitive data on interval PC development post-resection
Best Practice Advice 6: Post-Resection With HGD or PC
  • HGD in resected specimen: MRI/MRCP surveillance
  • Every 6 months for 2 years
  • Then annually, as long as surgical candidate for completion pancreatectomy
  • PC in resected specimen: follow oncologic guidelines and treatment course
Long-term Considerations
  • Physicians should discuss discontinuation after 5 years stability
  • No development of worrisome features or high-risk stigmata
  • Requires oncology team consultation
IAP Post-Resection Guidelines
  • Annual surveillance for all noninvasive IPMN (LGD) in resected specimen
  • 6-month surveillance if family history of PC or HGD present
Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) Surveillance Overview
  • ~8.1% of Medicare population has cirrhosis diagnosis
  • Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis driving new HCC diagnoses
  • Age increases HCC risk independent of fibrosis stage
  • 24% of older adults with cirrhosis undiagnosed during lifetime (autopsy series)
Best Practice Advice 7: Viral Hepatitis → HCC Risk Persists Despite Treatment
  • Oral antivirals lower but do not eliminate HCC risk
HBV Suppression
  • Nucleoside/nucleotide analogues → 40%–50% reduction in HCC risk
HCV Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs)
  • Up to 70% HCC risk reduction with sustained virologic response
  • Particularly effective in compensated cirrhosis
DAA Selection in Older Adults
  • Consider polypharmacy and chronic kidney disease
  • Check for drug–drug interactions (DDIs)
  • Renal monitoring essential
Dosing Adjustments
Drug Adjustment
Tenofovir alafenamide No adjustment if CrCl >15 mL/min
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate Requires renal adjustment
Entecavir Requires renal adjustment
Preferred Agents
  • Entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide preferred over tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (bone mineral density concerns)
HCV DAA Drug Interactions
  • Protease inhibitors (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir): high interaction with:
  • Statins (atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin)
  • Enalapril
  • Digoxin
  • Angiotensin-receptor blockers
  • NS5A/NS5B inhibitors (sofosbuvir, ledipasvir, daclatasvir, velpatasvir): lower DDI risk
  • Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir + amiodarone: contraindicated (life-threatening bradycardia)
  • High-risk medication classes: antiplatelets, PPIs, HIV therapies, antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, anticonvulsants
Resource
  • Liverpool HEP Interactions: https://www.hepdruginteractions.org/
Best Practice Advice 8: Cirrhosis → Consider HCC Surveillance
  • Age >75 years with cirrhosis of any etiology → consider surveillance
  • Age increases HCC risk
  • Exception: life expectancy <1–2 years
Rationale for Surveillance Continuation
  • Older adults more likely to develop cirrhosis (progressive liver damage over time)
  • Identifying HCC early → access to curative therapies:
  • Resection
  • Ablation
  • Transplantation
Factors Guiding Surveillance Decisions
  • Liver disease stage (Child-Pugh class)
  • Functional status
  • Comorbidities
  • Transplant candidacy
No Absolute Age Cutoffs for Liver Transplant
  • Waitlist and post-transplant outcomes inferior in:
  • Older adults
  • Those with impaired functional status
  • Patients on dialysis
  • High comorbidity burden
Surveillance Still Valuable Without Transplant Option
  • Locoregional therapy outcomes similar in age ≥80 vs <80 years (e.g., TACE)
  • Child-Pugh A or B with good performance status → systemic therapy options
Best Practice Advice 9: Stop Surveillance if Life Expectancy <1–2 Years
  • Life expectancy <1–2 years → stop HCC surveillance
  • Based on:
  • Medical comorbidities
  • Impaired functional status
  • Liver decompensation (e.g., Child-Turcotte-Pugh C cirrhosis)
  • Liver transplant not an option
Shared Decision-Making
  • Patients can inform HCC surveillance decisions
  • Individualized approach based on:
  • Liver disease severity (Child-Pugh A, B, or C if transplant available)
  • Performance status (ECOG 0–1)
  • Comorbidities
Key Assessment Tools
AACCI (Age-Adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index)
  • Most common comorbidity assessment in PCL literature
  • Used to assess surgery impact on patients with PCLs
Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) Classification
  • Used for liver disease staging
  • Determines cirrhosis severity
  • CTP Class C → surveillance not beneficial if transplant unavailable
ECOG Performance Status
Score Definition
0 Fully active, no restrictions
1 Strenuous physical activity restricted
2 Ambulatory, able to carry out light work
3 Capable of only limited self-care, in bed >50% of waking hours
4 Completely disabled, fully confined
  • ECOG ≥3 → symptomatic patient in bed at least 50% of waking hours
Guidelines Comparison: When to Stop PCL Surveillance
Guideline At Detection After 5y Stable Post-LGD Resection Post-HGD Resection
AGA 2015 Clear risk discussion Yes, if no change or not surgical candidate No surveillance MRI every 2y or more frequent
ACG 2018 No evaluation if medically unfit If no longer surgical candidate Lifelong if surgically fit MRI or EUS every 6 mo
European 2018 No follow-up if unfit N/A (lifelong in fit) Lifelong if surgically fit Every 6 mo for 2y, then yearly
ACR 2020 <5 mm: stop at 2y if stable Minimum 5–10 y follow-up If surgically fit Continued surveillance
Kyoto 2024 Consider stopping ≤2 cm, no change after 5y Yes Lifelong every y Every 6 mo
Key Statistics Summary
PCL Risk in Elderly
  • 26%–38% of patients >70 years have incidental PCLs
  • Only 0.9% of stable PCLs ≤1.5 cm for >5 years develop PC
  • 4.8% of PCLs ≤1.0 cm developed worrisome features with prolonged surveillance
  • Up to 44% of PC in IPMN patients may be concomitant (unrelated)
Surgery Outcomes
  • 1%–4% mortality in expert centers
  • 40%–50% adverse event rate
  • 17.1%/23.7% new diabetes after Whipple/distal pancreatectomy
HCC Risk Reduction
  • HBV suppression: 40%–50% reduction
  • HCV DAA achievement of SVR: up to 70% reduction

Post resection, International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) guidelines recommend annual surveillance for all noninvasive IPMN (LGD) in the resected specimen and 6-month surveillance when there is family history of PC, as long as the patient remains surgically fit.27
Figure 2: Surveillance algorithm of HCC in the elderly. AFP, alpha fetoprotein; CTP, Child-Turcotte-Pugh; ECOG, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status; US, ultrasound. *HBV patients at high-risk of HCC without cirrhosis: PAGE-B score ≥10 (composed of age, sex, and platelet count); age 50 or older for women and 40 or older for men if born in countries where HBV is endemic (highest endemicity in East, North, Southeast Asia, most of the Middle East and Eastern Europe), persons born in Africa due to aflatoxin B1 exposure; family history of HCC. **There are no absolute age cutoffs to stop HCC surveillance. ECOG score of 3 or greater indicates a patient who is symptomatic and in bed at least 50% of waking hours.
